title: Medellín: Heart of Downtown
summary: From the giant brick cathedral to Botero's plaza and the Park of Lights: how a small colonial town became Colombia's city of reinvention.
intro: Welcome to downtown Medellín, El Centro. Over the next two hours we'll walk from the cathedral, through the old shopping streets, past Botero's famous sculptures, to the Park of Lights, and finish at a square with a powerful story about peace. A few tips before we start. Do this walk in the daytime, ideally on a weekday when the streets are full of life. Keep your phone in your pocket between stops, and your bag in front of you. Locals have a saying for this: no dar papaya, don't make it easy. Now, let's go.

stops.name: Metropolitan Cathedral
stops.text: Look up at this enormous church. This is the Metropolitan Cathedral of Medellín, and it's one of the largest churches in the world built almost entirely of brick, more than a million of them. It was designed by the French architect Charles Émile Carré, and it took about fifty years to build, finally finishing in 1931. In front of it is Bolívar Park, named after Simón Bolívar, the general who led much of South America to independence from Spain. That's him on horseback. Now walk to the corner of the park and head south, down the pedestrian street called Junín.

stops.name: Down Junín
stops.text: This is the Pasaje Junín. A hundred years ago, walking up and down this street in your best clothes was the fashionable thing to do. People even made a verb out of it: juniniar, to go strolling on Junín. Look out for the old bakeries and cafés along the way. Some of them have been serving pastries and hot chocolate for generations. Keep walking south. You'll soon see a very tall building shaped like a needle.

stops.name: Coltejer Building
stops.text: This needle-shaped tower is the Coltejer building, finished in 1972, and still the tallest building in Medellín. Its shape is a nod to the company that built it, Coltejer, a giant textile maker. In the twentieth century Medellín became the industrial capital of Colombia, and textiles were its engine. Thousands of people, many of them women, worked in the fabric mills. That spirit of hard work is something people from this region, the paisas, are very proud of. Now turn right, west, and walk one block to the square with the metro running above it.

stops.name: Berrío Park
stops.text: Welcome to Berrío Park, the oldest square in the city. Medellín was officially founded around here in 1675, with the name Villa de Nuestra Señora de la Candelaria. That's why the white church on the side of the square is the Candelaria church, dedicated to the city's patron. Above you runs the metro. Medellín's metro opened in 1995, and it's still the only metro in Colombia. People here are so proud of it that they talk about cultura metro: no graffiti, no litter, everyone keeps it spotless. Look for the large bronze woman by the bank. She's a Botero, and locals call her La Gorda. Now walk north one block to a plaza full of more of his sculptures.
stops.credit: José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Plaza Botero
stops.text: This is Plaza Botero. Fernando Botero was born in Medellín in 1932 and became one of the most famous artists in the world, known for his round, oversized people and animals. He gave the city these twenty three bronze sculptures, and the plaza opened in 2002. Walk around and find your favourite: the horse, the cat, Adam and Eve. Botero always said his figures weren't fat, they were about volume and sensuality. The big building behind them is the Museum of Antioquia, once the city hall, and inside are many more of his paintings, plus works he donated by other artists. Botero died in 2023, and this square is his gift to his hometown.
stops.credit: Steffen Schmitz (more photos), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Palace of Culture
stops.text: Now turn to the black and white checkered building that looks like a castle. This is the Palace of Culture Rafael Uribe Uribe. It was designed in the 1920s by a Belgian architect, Agustín Goovaerts, in a Gothic revival style. It was meant to be the regional government's headquarters, but it was never finished as planned, and the government later moved out. Today it's a cultural centre, with exhibitions and archives, and entry is often free, so peek inside if it's open. From here, head south along Carabobo, the long pedestrian street. Stay alert in the crowds.

stops.name: Along Carabobo
stops.text: This is Carabobo, one of the busiest streets in downtown, packed with street vendors, small shops and music. It's the real, everyday Medellín. If you're hungry, look for a fresh fruit cart. Try mango biche, green mango with lime and salt, or a cup of fresh lulo or maracuyá juice. Keep walking south for a few blocks. We're heading for an old brick building with arches.

stops.name: Vásquez and Carré buildings
stops.text: These two handsome brick buildings with arches are the Vásquez and Carré buildings, from the late eighteen hundreds. Remember Charles Carré, the architect of the cathedral? He designed these too. Back then this was the edge of Guayaquil, the city's buzzing commercial district, full of markets, warehouses and travellers arriving by train. Over the years the area became run down, but these buildings were rescued and restored as part of the city's renewal. Just ahead you'll see a forest of tall white poles.

stops.name: Park of Lights
stops.text: Welcome to the Park of Lights. Those three hundred tall poles light up at night, like a forest of light. This square was once called Plaza Cisneros, the heart of the old Guayaquil market area. For years it had a reputation for crime. In the early two thousands, the city transformed it, adding this park and the library you see next to it. That was the big idea behind Medellín's famous turnaround: put the most beautiful public buildings in the places that needed them most. Look at the library on your right.
stops.credit: Jorge Láscar from Australia, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: EPM Library
stops.text: This dramatic building, shaped like an upside down pyramid, is the EPM Library, opened in 2005. EPM is the city's public utility company, and it's owned by the city itself, which is unusual. Its profits help pay for libraries, parks and schools across Medellín. Libraries like this one became symbols of the city's change. Medellín went from being called one of the most dangerous cities in the world, in the early nineteen nineties, to winning awards as one of the most innovative. The library is free, so feel free to go in and cool off. Then look across the road, to the old railway station.

stops.name: Old railway station
stops.text: This elegant building was the main station of the Antioquia Railway. In the late eighteen hundreds, a Cuban engineer, Francisco Javier Cisneros, began building a railway to connect Medellín, high in the mountains, with the Magdalena River, and from there, the sea. Before the railway, goods came up on mule trains along steep trails. The train brought coffee out and the modern world in, and helped turn Medellín into an industrial city. The old Plaza Cisneros you just saw was named after him. The trains are gone now, but the station has been preserved. Now head east, about five blocks, to our last stop, San Antonio Park.

stops.name: Walk to San Antonio
stops.text: As you walk, a quick word about the paisas, the people of this region. They're known across Colombia for being entrepreneurial, chatty and very proud of where they come from. You'll hear words like parce, meaning friend, and qué más, meaning how are you. If someone helps you, say muchas gracias, and you'll probably hear con mucho gusto, with great pleasure. Keep going east. The big open park is just ahead.

stops.name: San Antonio Park and the birds
stops.text: Find the two bronze birds by Botero, side by side. In June 1995, during a free concert here, a bomb hidden under the first bird exploded, killing more than twenty people. Botero asked the city not to remove the broken bird. He wanted it to stay as a reminder of the violence. A few years later, he placed a new, complete bird right next to it, and called it the Bird of Peace. Standing here, you can see Medellín's story in two sculptures: the wound, and the hope. Thank you for walking with me through El Centro. For a well earned break, the El Poblado tour is the perfect next step. Gracias, and enjoy Medellín.
stops.credit: Felipe Restrepo Acosta, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
